title: How do hospitals and health systems work, and what matters in a healthcare case?
description: Healthcare economics for case interviews: capacity, beds, length of stay, patient flow, payers and public goals, with a worked bed-capacity example.
hook: Hospitals turn fixed capacity (beds, operating theatres, staff) into treated patients, and they are paid by governments, insurers or patients under rules that decide whether treating more patients, or treating them faster, earns more money. A healthcare case usually tests capacity and patient flow, who pays and how, and your judgement about quality and safety, because the goal is often better care within a budget rather than maximum profit.
body:
Who pays and what success means

Depending on the country, care is paid for by the government (as with the NHS in the UK), by insurers (private insurers, or public programmes such as Medicare in the US) or by patients themselves. Before structuring, ask who the client is and what it is trying to achieve. A public hospital wants shorter waits, better outcomes and a balanced budget. A private hospital group also wants growth and margin. Do not force a profit lens onto a public goal (see public sector cases).

How the hospital is paid changes the economics:

  • Fee for service: paid for each test, procedure or day. More activity means more revenue.
  • Fixed payment per admission: a set amount for a type of case, whatever the length of stay. Shorter stays mean more margin. Medicare's inpatient system in the US works broadly this way, using diagnosis-related groups.
  • Fixed budget or per-person payment: the provider gets a set sum for a population, so keeping people well and out of hospital is what saves money.

The measures that matter

  • Bed occupancy and average length of stay.
  • Waiting times at each stage, both the median and the longest waits.
  • Readmission rates and other outcome measures, which show whether faster care is still good care.
  • Staffing levels, agency staff use and cost per treated patient.

A worked example: why length of stay matters

An illustrative ward has 30 beds. It cannot run at 100% every night and still absorb emergencies and discharge delays, so assume it averages 85% occupancy (an often-quoted planning rule of thumb, though researchers debate the exact figure).

  • Occupied bed-days a year: 30 × 365 × 85% ≈ 9,308.
  • At an average stay of 6 days: 9,308 ÷ 6 ≈ 1,551 patients a year.
  • At 5 days: 9,308 ÷ 5 ≈ 1,862 patients, about 20% more with the same beds.

Cutting a day off the average stay creates the equivalent of six extra beds. But only if the shorter stay is safe: premature discharge shows up later as readmissions. A good recommendation tests both throughput and quality.

The payment model matters too. Suppose a hospital receives a fixed $9,000 per admission for a condition and each bed-day costs it $1,500. At a 6-day stay it breaks even ($9,000 − 6 × $1,500 = $0). At 5 days it earns $1,500 per patient. Under a per-day payment, the same improvement would cut revenue. Always ask how the client is paid before assuming faster is better for its finances.

A quick tool: beds needed

Average beds occupied = admissions per day × average length of stay. If a ward admits 5 patients a day who stay 6 days, about 30 beds are occupied on average. To keep occupancy at 85%, it needs 30 ÷ 0.85 ≈ 35 beds. This one line (Little's law) answers a surprising number of capacity questions.

Emergency department waits

Draw the patient journey: arrival, triage, tests, treatment, decision, then discharge or admission. Ask at which step the queue has grown. If 12 patients arrive an hour at peak but four doctors each see 2.5 an hour (10 an hour), the queue grows by 2 patients an hour: 12 extra waiting after a 6-hour peak. Often, though, the real bottleneck is downstream: admitted patients wait in the emergency department because no inpatient bed is free. More triage nurses will not fix that (worked through in the operations case guide).

Typical healthcare case questions

  • Why have emergency waiting times doubled?
  • How can a hospital cut costs without harming care?
  • Should we add consultation rooms, or use the ones we have better?
  • How should a private hospital group double revenue in five years?
  • Why is a new drug selling below forecast? (see pharma cases)

What a strong answer sounds like

Weak: "To cut waiting times, the hospital should hire more doctors."
Strong: "Before adding staff, I'd find the bottleneck. If patients are waiting for a bed after the decision to admit, the constraint is inpatient discharge, not the emergency department, so I'd look at length of stay and weekend discharges."

Common mistakes

  • Assuming capacity is just the number of beds. Staff, theatres, diagnostics and discharge processes all limit throughput.
  • Planning for 100% occupancy. Real demand fluctuates. A full ward has no room for the next emergency.
  • Treating speed as the goal. Pair every efficiency measure with a quality one, such as readmissions.
  • Forgetting patients and staff. Interviewers expect you to mention safety, staff workload and patient experience without being prompted.

Practise

1. A ward admits 8 patients a day with an average stay of 4.5 days. How many beds does it need to run at 85% occupancy?

Show the answer

Average occupied beds: 8 × 4.5 = 36. Beds needed: 36 ÷ 0.85 ≈ 42 beds.

2. A clinic has 10 clinicians, each with 20 slots a day, 240 days a year, at $120 a slot. 10% of patients do not turn up. What do no-shows cost a year?

Show the answer

Slots: 10 × 20 × 240 = 48,000. No-shows: 10% = 4,800. Lost revenue: 4,800 × $120 = $576k a year, since clinician time is a fixed cost. Reminders, a waiting list for short-notice slots or careful overbooking could recover part of it.

3. A health system wants to cut average length of stay from 6 days to 5. What would you check before backing the plan?

Show the answer

Whether there is demand to fill the freed beds, how the hospital is paid (per admission or per day), whether readmissions or complications rise, whether community and social care can take patients earlier, and what it means for staff workload. Pilot it on one ward and track waits, readmissions and cost per patient.

Where to practise next

The casebook has several healthcare cases: Westmoor Clinic (will more rooms cut waits?), Summit Dialysis (making room on a full schedule), Willow Physio (the cost of no-shows) and Meridian Hospitals (doubling a hospital group's revenue).
